nameStory: The Thicklip Ramshorn gets its name from two distinctive features that make it stand out among freshwater snails. Its shell spirals flat like a ram's horn, coiling in the same plane rather than forming a tall spire. The 'thicklip' part refers to the notably thick, reinforced edge around the shell opening, which feels sturdy compared to other delicate aquatic snails.
description: The Thicklip Ramshorn is a small freshwater snail that lives in ponds, streams, and wetlands throughout New England. Its most striking feature is its distinctive flat, disk-shaped shell that coils in a tight spiral, resembling a miniature ram's horn when viewed from above. These snails are typically brown to amber in color and small enough to sit comfortably on your fingertip. Like other ramshorn snails, they're peaceful grazers that help keep aquatic environments clean by eating algae and decaying plant matter.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: The shell coils flat in one plane like a tiny cinnamon roll, rather than spiraling upward into a cone shape like most snails

idTips.label: Shell Opening
idTips.description: The opening has a noticeably thick, reinforced rim that feels solid when you gently touch it with your finger

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shell ranges from light brown to amber, sometimes with darker growth lines visible as faint rings around the spiral

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to fit on your thumbnail, typically measuring less than half an inch across

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Shell surface feels smooth but not glossy, with a slightly chalky texture when dry

habitat: Thicklip Ramshorns prefer quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow-moving streams, marshes, and wetland edges throughout New England. They're often found clinging to submerged rocks, fallen logs, or aquatic plants in shallow water where sunlight can reach the bottom. Look for them in areas with soft sediment and plenty of decaying organic matter, which provides their main food source.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge as water temperatures rise, often seen grazing on early algae growth on rocks and submerged surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when snails are most visible and shells are easiest to spot on pond edges and shallow water areas.
seasonality.fall: Snails remain active but may move to deeper water as temperatures drop, though empty shells often wash up on shores.
seasonality.winter: Living snails retreat to deeper water or bury in sediment, but shells can still be found along ice-free shorelines.

funFact: Ramshorn snails can actually breathe air and water, carrying a bubble of air inside their shell like a built-in scuba tank, which they can use to stay underwater for extended periods while grazing on the bottom of ponds!
confusionNotes: Other ramshorn snails in the same family look very similar, but the Thicklip's notably thick shell rim is the key difference - run your finger around the opening and you'll feel how much sturdier it is compared to the thin, delicate edges of other ramshorn species.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'ramshorn' can be confusing because it refers to an entire family of flat-coiled freshwater snails, not just one species. When people say 'ramshorn snail,' they might be referring to any of several different species that all share this distinctive flat-spiral shell shape.
compareHints: Since this is the only Planorbula species in our region, compare it to other ramshorn snails in the Planorbidae family. The Thicklip Ramshorn is distinguished by its reinforced shell opening and typically smaller size. Other ramshorn snails in New England tend to have thinner shell lips and may grow larger, but they share the same basic flat-coiled shell design.
